en: Having prostrated before the Guru Śiva— the omniscient, the creator of all, and the soul of all— I shall, O Śaunaka, declare the characteristics of the pronunciation of phonemes according to the Ṛk-śikṣā. 1.

The definition of the Veda, which increases the intelligence of children, has been stated correctly according to the ancient treatises; it is thus summarized here for its meaningfulness. Indeed, the collection of phonemes is of two kinds: vowels and consonants.
The vowels are to be known as beginning with *a*, and the consonants are said to begin with *ka*. The vowel is to be understood as being of two kinds: nasal (*nāsikya*) and resonant (*anunāsika*).
Furthermore, there are [four types]: acute (*udātta*), grave (*anudātta*), circumflex (*svarita*), and protracted (*pracaya*).
The five groups beginning with *ka* are designated as "contacts" (*sparśa*).

It should be understood that the letter *ḍa*, when situated between vowels, is called "lightly contacted" (*duḥspṛṣṭa*). The first letters of the groups are [the stops], while the second letters are designated as "sibilants" (*ūṣman*).
With the exception of the letter *ha*, the remaining unvoiced consonants are called "voiced. The five nasalized letters (*nāsikya*),
as well as the *anusvāra* and the four *yamas*, are declared to be indistinct and nasalized.
The four semivowels beginning with *y*, the four nasals (*nāsikya*) excluding *r*,
the four sibilants (*ūṣman*) beginning with *ś*, and the two [aspirate] spirants— the *jihvāmūlīya* and the *upadhmānīya*— are thus proclaimed. (8)
The two [vowels] resting on *k* (the *ka-varga*) are born from heat (*ūṣman*), as are the two possible occurrences of the *visarga*.
Short, long, and protracted—these vowels are designated by their duration;
the duration of the diphthongs (*saṃdhyakṣara*) consists of the long and protracted [vowels], and is not measured by a single *mātrā*.

The consonants have half a mora (*mātrā*), and the *svarabhakti* is likewise; in the case of a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*), the *svarabhakti* is proclaimed to have a quarter-mora (*pāda-mātrā*). However, an *anusvāra* following a short vowel is proclaimed to have three-quarters of a mora.
That short [vowel] shall consist of three quarters; these two [the long and the protracted] are equal in measure.

The *anusvāra* following a long [vowel] is proclaimed to be one quarter [of a mātrā]; that [quarter] added to the long [vowel] constitutes what is called the duration of a syllable (*varṇakāla*). 12–13.

The vowels *a*, *u*, and *ha* are said to be produced from the throat (*kaṇṭhaja*), and the *visarga* is also produced from the throat. The sounds *i*, *e*, *ca*, *ya*, and *śa* are born from the palate (*tālavya*). The retroflex sounds *ṛ*, *ṭ*, *u*, *ra*, and *ṣa* are traditionally taught as being produced from the roof of the mouth (*mūrdhan*).
The dentals *lṛ*, *ta*, *la*, and *sa* are said to be produced from the teeth (*dantya*). The *upadhmānīya* is produced from the lips (*oṣṭhaja*).
One should know that *u* and *ū* are labial; likewise, *vo* is both dental and labial.
*E* and *ai* are produced from the throat and palate (*kaṇṭhatālavyau*), while *o* and *au* are remembered as being produced from the throat and lips (*kaṇṭhoṣṭhajau*).
The manner of articulation (*karaṇa*) for the stops (*sparśānām*) is "contact" (*spṛṣṭam*), whereas for the semivowels (*antasthāsu*) it is said to be "slight" (*īṣat*). 15–16.

The articulation of the vowels and the sibilants is traditionally held to be open (vivṛta), while that of the letter *a* is closed (saṃvṛta); thus all phonemes are described. [In the case] of *o*, *au*, and the *u*-vowels, as well as when several [of these] meet together—

One should recognize that the two labials [p and ph] are pronounced together as a single sound if there is no other vowel between them, as in *uṣo na* and *oṣūṇo agne*. The [labial] *yuyotu* and *yūyuviḥ* [are treated similarly].
Furthermore, when there is a pause (*virāma*) or a hiatus (*vivṛtti*), if there are two consonants in the middle, [the preceding labial is also combined]. (18–19)
One should separate the two lips at the sound of *va*, and likewise the lower lip at *vakāra*;
thus one should utter "yanmayobhu" and "tābhirūṣu ūtibhiḥ," "bhrātuḥ putrān," "dhenum somaḥ," and "suṣṭutirmoṣu vo asmat."
Where *kutapva* [ants] are constantly seen at the joints,
if they are occupied by their own kind, one should cause a hero to be made right there with the verses "jyok karat," "uttarāham," "uttara," and "imam ma. (21–22)

The letter *na* at the end of a word is elided before the letter *ra*, the semivowels (*antasthā*), and the sibilants (*ūṣman*), provided it is preceded by the vowel *ā*; however, when followed by *sa* or *śa*, both [the *na* and the preceding *ā*] are elided. Furthermore, the nasal (*nāsikya*) is the substitute for the preceding vowel, and that is proclaimed to be the *raṅga*.

As it was in his former time when he was ruling, so it is now: "O Indu, I am being struck down by Dasyus; I am reaching the lowliest Panis. Protect me from them as I cry out; guard both them and my sons. (24–25)
The substitution of *ṇṛn* for *nṝn*, *pe* for *pāyau*, and the elision (*visarga*) are prescribed;
furthermore, the nasalization (*raṅga*) of a vowel not preceded by *n* may occasionally occur before a vowel. Examples:
*nṝm̐ pātram*, *svatavām̐ pāyuḥ*, *savāyam̐ eva sa cām̐ indraḥ*.
The long vowel and the prolated vowel at the end of a word are elided before the syllable *uḥ*.
(27) This rule has been declared for the end of a word, yet it is also observed within a word, as in the examples *abhūd upāram* and *ubhā ūnūnaṃ vindati*. (28)
In the words *māṃspacanyām*, *māṃścatve*, and *hrasvatve*, as well as in the forms *mam̐ścataḥ* where the *m* is at the end of a word, the *anusvāra* indeed occurs when followed by *r*,
a sibilant (*ūṣman*), or any other consonant, even when occurring in the middle of a word. 29.
They urge that chariot forward for you; you [attain] that fame when the bright juice is pressed.
On the sixth day, which has a common ending, one alone carves the flesh, as does the fifth among his own group, regarding both the objects of touch and the sense-objects.
And among the semivowels (antasthā), those same [nasals] are prescribed for the letter *m*. For example:
*idaṃ kaveḥ*, *taṃ gīrbhiḥ*, *nakiṣṭaṃ ghnanti*, *jaṅghanataḥ* (32), *sañcodaya*, *sañjānānān*, *tantum ātan*, *devāḥ śannaḥ*.
And [the rules] "tvam pavitre," "prataram lāyam," and "tayat saṃvardhata" [apply].
Furthermore, if a conjunction of consonants occurs with one another, there is no hearing of the preceding [vowel] in the case of a pause or a consonant. 33–34.
Vākpūtā, Vāgdevī, Viṭkulā, Dvibhrāt, Bṛhat, Tatpunarjaṅghnanti, Triṣṭub, Gāyatrī, and Arvāgvit— anuṣṭubh follows after these. Indeed,
when joined with the fifth of the *sparśa* (stop) consonants, they are recorded as being *yamās*.
That which is equal to a lump of iron is proclaimed as having dense bonds (ghanabandha).
We know the aged women, the jewels of sacrifice, and the attainment of wealth;
likewise, the *sparśa* letters and the fifth class [the nasals] are joined with the semi-vowels (*antasthā*). 36–37.

That which is like a block of wood is proclaimed as *ghanabandha*; *saravya*, *kṛcchra*, *vajra*, *rāṣṭrya*, *atīḍya*, and *samrāj* [are also types]. *Mīḍhvān*, *tathyam*, *vādhryaśva*, *utāpamlukta*, and *vibhvī* are likewise mentioned. 38.

The sibilants (ūṣman), when joined with the fifth letters [the nasals] and combined with the semivowels (antasthā), are proclaimed to have a loose articulation (ślathabandha), being similar to a mass of wool (ūrṇāpiṇḍa).
Examples include "aśnotu," "viṣṇurghṛtasnu," "asme," "yuṣme," and "snuṣe. (39–40)
In the verse "asya vāmasyājuṣran," the word "aśva" is joined with "sammiśla";
furthermore, the letter *va* is here joined with both *na* and *ṇa*.
This should be understood as having a loose articulation (*ślathabandha*), and it is also called "difficult to touch" (*duḥspṛṣṭa*) in this context. 41
When the *visarjanīya* occurs before the two *kap* sounds (*k* and *p*),

it does not undergo [elision] in *saṃhitā* when followed by a pair of sibilants (*ūṣman*). Where *ṛ* or *ḷ* vowels precede and sibilants (*ūṣman*) stand as the subsequent [sounds], [the rule applies].
The *svarabhakti* is proclaimed as a fraction of the preceding vowel.
One should know that the letter *ha*, when joined with the fifth [consonants] and the semivowels (*antasthā*), is guttural (*urasya*), provided it is pronounced separately after them. (43–44)
From the first [consonant], one obtains the letter *ha*, which is the fourth;
then one obtains its own third [consonant], for that is indeed the preceding letter.
Due to the combination with an *anusvāra* or a vowel, the beginning of a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*) is pronounced twice.
The first two [letters] of the *ūṣman* group are to be known as following the letter *la*; likewise, the other [letter], *sparśa*, follows it.
The letters *na* and *ṅa*, preceded by a short vowel, undergo doubling when a vowel follows. Furthermore, after the first *na*, either the letter *śa* or the *cha*-sound (*chatva*) occurs. 46–47.
In this [section], after a short vowel, there are two *c*s, and after a long vowel, one is also seen;
[these occur] in the word *pavamāna* along with that which has *sa*, excluding *ati* and *hāya*. When *s* follows *ṇ* and *ṭ*, a *t* is produced in the middle.

In the case of *na* and *ta*, as well as in the *la* and *ca* groups, there is homogeneity (*savarṇa*) with the following [consonant]. However, when followed by a vowel that is designated as "voiced" (*ghoṣavat*), the first letters at the end of a word optionally attain their third [consonant of the same class], and likewise, the fifth letters attain their fifth.
When followed by a sibilant (*ūṣman*), the first sounds at the end of a word are to be understood as second sounds by those who know phonetics.
The letters *ya* and *ra*, when joined with the letter *ṛ*, [behave in this manner]. 51.
In that state, the lips should not tremble; this is quickly explained as follows:

the sound is heard through resonance (*ghoṣa*), cessation (*virāma*), and likewise through doubling (*dvitva*); thus, from the nature of the phonemes, there arises that which is neither nasal nor nasal (*anāsikya*).
That which is low-pitched is called *anudātta* (unaccented), and that which is high-pitched is called *udātta* (accented).
The combination of these two is *svarita* (circumflex), and their unification is known as *pracaya* (continuous accent).
The *anudātta* should be understood as being in the heart, while the *udātta* is said to be in the head.

The *svarita* [accent] is located at the root of the ear; in all other cases, it is remembered as *pracaya*. One should cause a tremor (*kampa*) in the middle, while both [the preceding and following syllables] should be low and equal.
For the purpose of the tremor, a duration twice that of a vowel-syllable is desired for the *pāda*.

Taking up an unaccented (anudātta) vowel, one should indeed support it with a circumflex (svarita), and then descend again to an unaccented tone; this is remembered as the rule for the "trembling" (kampa).
In this case, the preceding portion is acute (udātta), while the subsequent portion is depressed (nihanyate).
It is called "acute intonation" (udāttakampa) and is observed in certain instances.
[The characteristics are: place, time, modification, closure, openness, slight contact, lack of voicing, vowel quality, intonation, and aspiration. 58–59.
These are considered to be the phonetic properties of voiced (*ghoṣa*), nasalized (*anāsikya*), and non-nasalized (*anāsikya*) sounds;
one should know that however many properties exist in a given place, there are exactly that many there.
The *praṇava* (the syllable Om) is proclaimed by the wise to consist of four morae (*mātrā*) and six morae.
The preceding vowel is known as the *svara* (vowel), while the subsequent sound (*nāda*) is proclaimed to have an equal duration.
The vowel is to be understood as *anudātta* (unaccented), and the *nāda* is called *udātta* (accented).
This is the definition of the *praṇava*; the *praṇava* is celebrated as Brahman.
He who knows that which is like an unbroken stream of oil, sounding like the long ring of a bell, unborn, and the pinnacle of the *praṇava*— he is a knower of the Veda.
It has three stations, three measures, is the triple Brahman, and consists of three syllables.
He who knows that which is half a mātrā within the three mātrās is a knower of the Veda.
For the Veda is indeed a collection of phonemes (varṇa), and the Veda is proclaimed as Brahman;
therefore, one who knows those phonemes of the Veda is glorified in the world of Brahman.
Knowing this merit— which removes sin and purifies the impurity of speech— and grasping it with devotion, one goes to the world of Brahmā.
He who studies the Veda according to this rule, endowed with faith, [attains the same].
Being liberated from all sins, he is glorified in the world of Brahmā. 67.
Thus ends the Śaunaka-śikṣā.
